title: The Smart Vehicle and the Factory of the Future
overview: Software, data and advanced manufacturing in China.

guide.objective: Understand how electrification, software, data and AI interact across vehicle architecture and factory operations.
procedure: Read each slide and state a prediction before changing any parameter.
Run the balanced baseline scenario and record output, rejects, work in process and OEE.
Change one parameter at a time: supply interval, buffer capacity or reliability.
Repeat with the same random seed, compare scenarios and explain the bottleneck.
Export the results and distinguish model output from external evidence.
guide.model: A discrete-event production line runs for 480 simulated minutes in 0.25-minute steps. Stations have cycle times, finite buffers, failures, repairs and quality rejects. Hourly reliability r is converted to a per-step failure probability: 1 − r^(Δt/60). Seed 20261115 makes runs reproducible. Ideal station capacity is 60 / cycle time (units per hour). Line OEE is an educational approximation based on the bottleneck station.
guide.limitations: The model discretizes time and is not calibrated to a real factory. The AI-factory scenario changes assumed parameters; it does not establish a causal effect of AI. Work in process includes queues and units being processed. Lost supply is recorded separately. OEE is not an audited BYD or industry metric.
questions: What happens when a station that is not the bottleneck becomes faster?
How much does predictive maintenance improve final good output?
What changes when buffer capacity is reduced?
Can OEE rise while the number of conforming vehicles falls?
guide.answers: Speeding up a non-bottleneck station may not increase final throughput. Buffers absorb variation but cannot remove a persistent capacity constraint. A technology investment matters only when it changes the binding constraint or reduces losses at the relevant stage.

slides.title: The Smart Vehicle and the Factory of the Future
slides.subtitle: Software, data and advanced manufacturing in China.
items: Architecture, driver assistance and over-the-air updates.
Robotics, quality control and production capacity.
slides.takeaway: How do these technologies work together to create value?
slides.notes: Open by connecting two systems: the vehicle and the factory that produces it. In both, sensors and software create value when they change a physical operation reliably. Electrification changes components and suppliers; the software-defined vehicle adds a platform that must be maintained for years. This convergence does not remove requirements for quality, safety or organization. Follow one decision: a camera detects an anomaly, a model interprets it, a person or controller acts, and a subsequent measurement verifies the result. The image is a conceptual illustration inherited from Class 1, not documentary photography of an identified plant. Return to the opening question during the final experiment.

slides.title: Four Industrial Transformations
slides.subtitle: Competitiveness depends on their integration.
items: Battery, power electronics, motor and charging.
Centralized or zonal computing, applications and OTA updates.
Perception, maintenance, planning and product improvement.
Robotics, logistics, traceability and quality control.
slides.takeaway: An isolated improvement can simply move the bottleneck.
slides.notes: Explain the transformations as distinct layers of one system. An electric vehicle need not provide advanced automated driving, and a robot-equipped plant need not use machine learning. Electrification, software, AI and automation therefore should not be used as synonyms. Ask for an example of complementarity: an update may improve charging management, but it still depends on battery and thermal limits; visual inspection may reduce defects, but traceability is needed to identify and correct their cause. Introduce the bottleneck: speeding up one station increases final output only if the other stations and the supply system can sustain the new rate. This provides a basis for evaluating a specific investment rather than counting installed technologies.

slides.title: The Software-Defined Vehicle
slides.subtitle: A conceptual architecture with updateable functions.
items: Sensors, actuators, battery and computing units.
Operating system, communications and separation of safety-critical functions.
Driver assistance, cockpit and services, each requiring specific validation.
Remote distribution with version management and cybersecurity.
slides.takeaway: Remote updates require safety validation throughout the vehicle life cycle.
slides.notes: Read the architecture from physical components to applications. Sensors and actuators connect software to the vehicle; the platform organizes communications, computing resources and separation of functions; applications add services that require their own validation. An OTA update is a distribution mechanism, not a safety guarantee. Explain the engineering sequence: identify version and vehicle, test compatibility, assess the change, deploy under control and retain traceability. A multimedia cockpit and a braking function have different criticality. Ask what would happen if an apparently minor change altered a response time. Software value also depends on the ability to maintain and audit it and to recover from an unsuccessful update.

slides.title: Huawei in the Automotive Ecosystem
slides.subtitle: A technology and platform supplier.
items: Sensors, perception, planning and control, depending on vehicle and version.
Data and updates subject to privacy and security requirements.
slides.takeaway: Distinguish the technology supplier, the vehicle manufacturer and the operator.
slides.notes: Use Huawei to illustrate how a technological value chain is organized, without confusing its role with that of every vehicle manufacturer. Sensors, computing, platforms, cockpit services and connectivity may come from different participants. The official ADS page warns that assistance does not replace the driver and that capabilities depend on model and available updates. A demonstration video shows selected conditions; it does not establish failure rates across all environments. Ask who integrates, validates, maintains and operates each function. In industrial economics, these decisions affect value capture, supplier dependence, interoperability and switching costs throughout the vehicle life cycle.

slides.title: Assistance, Automation and Responsibility
slides.subtitle: Who performs the task and who handles fallback
items: The person performs or supervises driving; L0 does not automate the task.
The system performs the driving task within its domain and may request intervention.
The system handles fallback within its operational domain.
Automation in all road conditions that a human driver could manage.
slides.takeaway: A commercial name does not establish the level of automation.
slides.notes: The SAE classification describes the allocation of the driving task and fallback; it does not by itself assign legal liability. At levels 0 to 2 the person retains driving supervision. At level 3 the system operates under defined conditions and may require a transition to the person. At level 4 the system handles fallback within its operational design domain; the function may be unavailable outside that domain. Level 5 requires broader scope. Define the domain using examples such as area, weather, speed and road characteristics. A product name or a successful maneuver does not establish a SAE level. Authorization and safety evidence must be assessed for the specific function and context.

slides.title: The Factory as a Production System
slides.subtitle: Availability × performance × quality, with an explicit unit of analysis
items: 60 / cycle time in minutes = units per hour.
Ideal cycle time × total units / operating time.
slides.takeaway: OEE = A × P × Q. Actual output also depends on supply and buffers.
slides.notes: Present OEE as availability multiplied by performance and quality, with an explicit unit of analysis. The chart uses a teaching example: 0.85 times 0.90 times 0.98 equals 0.7497, or approximately 75%. If a station has an ideal capacity of 120 units per hour, this corresponds to about 90 good units per hour under compatible assumptions; it does not automatically predict plant output. Supply, buffers, shared stoppages and bottlenecks can change the result. Do not average machine OEE percentages as though they were aggregate production. As adoption context, IFR reported 354,000 new robot installations in China in 2025, representing 59% of global installations. Installation and productivity remain different indicators.

slides.title: Value Chains and Geoeconomics
slides.subtitle: Costs and capabilities are distributed across sectors.
items: Electric grid, charging, standards and trade.
slides.takeaway: For Latin America, identify concrete capabilities before inferring opportunities.
slides.notes: Follow the value chain from materials to services. Possessing a mineral resource does not mean controlling chemical processing, cell manufacturing or vehicle integration. Software does not remove those physical capabilities. Introduce three questions for Latin America: what local problem exists, what complementary capability can be developed, and what access to data and maintenance is required? Diagnostics or charging management may require less capital than a cell plant but still depend on connectivity, standards and supplier agreements. Use IEA trade evidence to distinguish manufacturing, domestic sales and exports. A high production share does not by itself establish profitability or the absence of technological dependence.

slides.title: Electric adoption: compare like with like
slides.subtitle: Share of new car sales in 2025, not share of the vehicle stock
slides.takeaway: Sales, production and fleet stock are different indicators.

side.label: electric cars sold in China in 2025

visual.caption: IEA, Global EV Outlook 2026. BEV + PHEV; 2025; rounded percentages.

slides.notes: The chart compares the electric share of new car sales in China, Europe and the United States in 2025. Values are rounded to 55%, 28% and approximately 10%; electric cars include battery electric and plug-in hybrid cars, rather than every vehicle marketed as a hybrid. These are annual sales shares, not the electric share of the vehicle stock on the road. The IEA records more than 13 million electric car sales in China that year. Ask why the sales share can grow rapidly while replacement of the fleet remains slower. Connect adoption with prices, model availability, charging and policy without assigning causality to a single variable. These are observed 2025 figures, not projections for 2030.

slides.title: Software and the physical limit
slides.subtitle: Ideal model: response distance plus braking distance
slides.takeaway: Doubling speed quadruples the braking component.

visual.caption: Teaching calculation in metres. μ = 0.7; g = 9.81 m/s²; no slope or aerodynamics.

slides.notes: This exercise reproduces the physical relationships used in the additional laboratory. At 60 km/h, speed is 16.67 m/s. With a one-second response and a friction coefficient of 0.7, response contributes about 16.7 meters and ideal braking about 20.2 meters. Doubling speed doubles response distance and quadruples the braking component. Removing the response second does not remove braking distance. Explain the units of speed times time and speed squared divided by twice friction times gravity. The chart is a teaching calculation, not a vehicle test or a safe-distance recommendation. It omits slope, aerodynamics, tire dynamics and perception failures. The aim is to identify the limit that software can change and the physical limit that remains.

slides.title: Summary and Experiment
slides.subtitle: A faster factory can still produce fewer good units.
items: Run the baseline and AI-factory scenarios with the same random seed.
Change buffer capacity, supply or reliability.
Record good units, rejects, WIP and OEE.
Identify whether the constraint is processing, supply or quality.
slides.takeaway: What changes when you optimize a station that is not the bottleneck?
slides.notes: Close with a controlled experiment. Ask students to run the baseline and AI-factory scenarios, record the seed and use the same eight-hour horizon. They should then change one variable: supply, reliability or buffers. Their submission should include good units, rejects, work in process and an explanation of the bottleneck. Higher OEE at one station can coexist with unchanged aggregate output. Connect this finding to the stopping-distance chart: in safety and production alike, a local improvement must be interpreted within the whole system. Ask for an investment decision and one condition under which it would no longer be worthwhile. Stating that condition makes the hypothesis explicit and supports discussion of evidence rather than technological promises.
